Title: Increased nucleated red blood cells counts in prolonged rupture of membranes is not erythropoietin driven.

Journal/Date: American journal of perinatology (2015)

MeSH Keywords: Adult, Body Mass Index, Cross-Sectional Studies, Erythrocyte Count, Erythropoietin, Female, Fetal Blood, Premature Rupture of Fetal Membranes


--- ABSTRACT ---
[OBJECTIVE]: The aim of this study is to examine the hypothesis that prolonged rupture of membranes (PROM) is associated with increased cord blood erythropoietin (EPO) concentrations, proportional to the duration of ruptured membranes.
[STUDY DESIGN]: This study is a prospective, cross-sectional, observational (noninterventional) cohort study of mother-infant pairs. Criteria for inclusion were as follows: active labor with or without ruptured membranes and vaginally delivered neonates. Excluded were infants with major factors known to be associated with a potential increase in fetal erythropoiesis.
[RESULTS]: A total of 40 mother-infant pairs were recruited. EPO was not influenced by duration of ruptured membranes and significantly correlated only with maternal body mass index.
[CONCLUSION]: Cord blood concentrations of EPO do not appear to be significantly affected by the duration of ruptured membranes. We speculate that erythropoiesis is upregulated in PROM by mechanisms that involve the production of cytokines and are not EPO driven.

NRBC counts were directly correlated with cord blood IL-6 levels (P < .001) but not with EPO, cortisol or parameters of acid-base status levels regardless of EONS status. These relationships remained following correction for gestational age, diabetes, intrauterine growth restriction, and steroid exposure.
[CONCLUSION]: In the setting of inflammation-associated preterm birth and in the absence of hypoxia, elevations in NRBCs in the early neonatal period may be a direct response of exposure to inflammatory mediators in utero.

=== PMID: 18776724 ===

Title: Increased fetal plasma and amniotic fluid erythropoietin concentrations: markers of intrauterine hypoxia.

Journal/Date: Neonatology (2009)

MeSH Keywords: Adult, Amniotic Fluid, Biomarkers, Erythropoietin, Female, Fetal Blood, Fetal Hypoxia, Humans


--- ABSTRACT ---
Tissue hypoxia is the major stimulus of erythropoietin (EPO) synthesis in fetuses and adults. Since EPO does not cross the placenta and is not stored, fetal plasma and amniotic fluid levels indicate EPO synthesis and elimination. Acutely, the rate and magnitude of the increase in plasma EPO levels correlate with the intensity of hypoxia. Amniotic fluid EPO levels correlate with cord plasma levels in normal and abnormal pregnancies, with fetal plasma EPO levels in humans averaging 2.6 times higher than the corresponding amniotic fluid EPO levels. Recent experimental and clinical studies demonstrate that EPO has neuroprotective effects related to its anti-apoptotic and vascular growth-promoting properties. Although under basal conditions the fetal kidneys are the main site of EPO production, during hypoxia recent experimental data indicate an important role of the placenta. Amniotic fluid EPO levels have been shown to increase exponentially during fetal hypoxia in preeclamptic, diabetic and Rh-immunized pregnancies, to correlate inversely with cord blood pH, pO(2) and base excess and to predict neonatal morbidities and NICU admission. As an indicator of chronic intrauterine hypoxia, fetal EPO measurements have increased our knowledge about the pathogenesis and importance of intrauterine growth restriction, macrosomia, diabetic pregnancy, prolonged pregnancy, meconium staining, fetal hemorrhage, fetal anemia, maternal smoking and alcohol consumption, abnormal fetal heart rate and abnormal Doppler flow patterns. While the clinical utility of fetal amniotic fluid and plasma EPO measurements in the management of high-risk pregnancies and their offspring is promising, adequately powered clinical trials are urgently needed.

key_findings.finding: The most direct PROM study (2015; 40 mother–infant pairs, prospective observational cohort, vaginal deliveries with active labor, excluding major causes of fetal erythropoiesis) found that cord-blood EPO was not associated with duration of ruptured membranes and correlated only with maternal BMI. Its conclusion was that PROM-associated erythropoiesis is likely cytokine-mediated and not EPO-driven; however, the abstract does not provide the numeric NRBC-by-PROM results or establish causality, and the sample was small and not specifically limited to PPROM.

source_tools.relevance: Direct PROM study measuring cord EPO and reporting its relationship to membrane duration

key_findings.finding: A 2008 study of 68 preterm singleton births, including 19 with early-onset neonatal sepsis and assessed for intra-amniotic inflammation, histologic chorioamnionitis, cord IL-6, EPO, cortisol, and acid-base status, found higher neonatal NRBC counts with EONS and a direct NRBC–cord IL-6 association, but no NRBC association with EPO, cortisol, or acid-base measures after adjustment. This supports an inflammation-associated, apparently EPO-independent NRBC response in preterm birth, though it was not a PROM-only cohort.

source_tools.relevance: Direct simultaneous measurement of NRBCs, IL-6, EPO, cortisol, and acid-base status

key_findings.finding: A 1997 study of 359 preterm infants delivered after preterm labor or PPROM found that clinical and histologic infection status were associated with increased NRBC counts; histologic chorioamnionitis remained significant after controlling for gestational age and birth-weight percentile, whereas clinical chorioamnionitis did not. The authors concluded that histologic chorioamnionitis produces a fetal erythropoietic response, but explicitly stated that the study could not determine whether this was due to inflammatory mediators directly or a rise in EPO.

source_tools.relevance: Large preterm/PPROM-associated cohort linking histologic chorioamnionitis to NRBCs while explicitly leaving EPO mediation unresolved

key_findings.finding: Hypoxia/EPO remains a biologically valid alternative pathway: in 300 high-risk newborns (gestational age 24–42 weeks), with NRBCs measured in 112, umbilical venous EPO correlated strongly with circulating NRBCs (r=0.74); EPO was elevated with acute villous circulatory disturbance, fetal vasculopathy, and chorioamnionitis with fetal reaction. The study concluded that hypoxia stimulates fetal EPO after a delay of several hours and increases erythropoiesis. This supports EPO-mediated NRBC elevation in hypoxic placental disease generally, but does not show that PROM duration or PPROM-associated NRBC elevation is EPO-mediated.

source_tools.relevance: Direct EPO–NRBC correlation and placental pathology study supporting hypoxia/EPO biology

key_findings.finding: A review of fetal plasma and amniotic-fluid EPO indicates that fetal EPO reflects intrauterine hypoxia and correlates with hypoxic markers such as lower cord pH, pO2, and base excess, but it does not directly test PROM/PPROM-associated NRBCs. Thus it provides mechanistic context rather than direct evidence for the PROM question.

source_tools.relevance: Mechanistic review of fetal EPO as a hypoxia biomarker

key_findings.finding: Overall, the direct evidence favors—but does not definitively prove—an EPO-independent mechanism for increased NRBCs in prolonged membrane rupture, especially when inflammation/chorioamnionitis is present: PROM duration did not raise cord EPO, and preterm inflammatory cohorts showed NRBC associations with IL-6/chorioamnionitis without EPO associations. Evidence is insufficient to exclude concurrent hypoxia/EPO effects in individual PPROM pregnancies, particularly with placental vascular pathology or fetal acidemia.

Evidence that hypoxia can raise EPO and NRBCs in other high-risk pregnancies

entities.name: PROM duration and EPO
observations: A prospective cohort of 40 mother–infant pairs found cord EPO was not associated with membrane-rupture duration; authors proposed cytokine-mediated erythropoiesis, but the small study did not establish causality.

source_tools.relevance: Direct PROM-duration and cord EPO evidence

entities.name: Inflammation and NRBCs
observations: In a preterm cohort, neonatal NRBCs associated with EONS and cord IL-6 but not EPO, cortisol, or acid-base measures after adjustment; cohort was not PROM-only.

source_tools.relevance: Inflammatory association and lack of EPO association

entities.name: Chorioamnionitis and NRBCs
observations: Among 359 preterm infants after preterm labor or PPROM, histologic chorioamnionitis associated with increased NRBCs after adjustment; study could not distinguish direct inflammation from EPO mediation.

entities.name: Hypoxia EPO NRBC pathway
observations: In a high-risk newborn cohort, umbilical EPO correlated with NRBCs (r=0.74), supporting hypoxia/EPO as an alternative pathway in placental disease, not specifically proving PROM mediation.

source_tools.relevance: Qualifies inference; establishes biologically plausible EPO pathway
